nameStory: The Eastern Comma gets its name from a tiny silver or white punctuation mark on the underside of its hindwings that looks exactly like a comma! This distinctive marking is so reliable that early naturalists used it as the defining characteristic when naming this butterfly. It's like nature signed its work with perfect punctuation.
description: The Eastern Comma is a medium-sized orange butterfly with deeply scalloped, ragged wing edges that make it look like a tattered autumn leaf. The upper wings are bright orange with bold black spots and borders, while the undersides are mottled brown and gray - perfect camouflage when the wings are closed. Adults have a wingspan of about 2-3 inches and belong to the brush-footed butterfly family, meaning their front legs are reduced and brush-like rather than used for walking. When perched with wings closed, they're nearly invisible against tree bark or fallen leaves.

idTips.label: Silver comma mark
idTips.description: Look for a bright silver or white comma-shaped mark on the underside of the hindwing - it's crisp and unmistakable, like someone painted punctuation on the wing

idTips.label: Ragged wing edges
idTips.description: Wings have deeply scalloped, irregular edges that feel rough to the touch and create a jagged silhouette unlike most other butterflies

idTips.label: Orange upper wings with black spots
idTips.description: Bright orange-brown upper wings decorated with bold black spots and thick black borders that catch the light when wings are spread

idTips.label: Mottled brown underwings
idTips.description: Undersides are cryptically colored in mottled browns, grays, and tans that perfectly mimic dead leaves or bark texture

idTips.label: Erratic flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with quick, jerky movements and sudden direction changes, often landing abruptly on tree trunks or the ground

habitat: Eastern Commas thrive in woodland edges, parks, gardens, and anywhere their host plants grow - especially areas with stinging nettles, elms, and hops. Look for them along forest margins, in suburban yards with mature trees, and near streams or clearings where sunlight filters through the canopy. They prefer semi-open areas where they can bask in sunny spots but quickly retreat to the shelter of trees.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hibernation and begin flying in March-April, looking somewhat faded and worn from overwintering. Fresh spring individuals start mating and laying eggs on emerging host plant leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity with fresh, bright adults flying from multiple generations. Look for them basking in sunny spots, visiting flowers, or sipping from rotting fruit and tree sap.
seasonality.fall: Later generation adults prepare for winter by finding sheltered spots under bark, in wood piles, or leaf litter. Colors may appear more intense as they build up reserves for hibernation.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate in protected spots and are occasionally seen on warm winter days, looking for sunny basking spots before returning to shelter.

funFact: Eastern Commas are living mood rings - they have two completely different seasonal forms, with fall individuals having much darker undersides than their spring and summer relatives, helping them blend in perfectly with autumn's changing colors!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Question Mark butterfly, which has a silver question mark (dot and curve) instead of a comma on its underwing. Remember: 'Comma has a comma, Question Mark has a question mark' - the punctuation marks are perfectly formed and easy to distinguish once you know to look for them.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Eastern' Comma, this species actually ranges across most of North America. The name distinguishes it from European comma species, and it was one of the first butterflies described by early American naturalists who were comparing New World species to their Old World counterparts.
compareHints: Among New England's comma butterflies, Eastern Comma is distinguished by its bright silver comma mark (Green Comma has a greenish tint underneath, Gray Comma is more muted overall, and Hoary Comma has a more irregular silver mark). Question Mark is larger with the distinctive curved silver question mark, while other Polygonia species are generally rarer and have subtly different underwing patterns and shapes to their silver punctuation marks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the comma butterflies, the Question Mark is the largest and the only one with the question mark punctuation mark on its underside.
Compared to the Eastern Comma, the Green Comma shows more greenish coloring on the underwing and tends to prefer more mountainous, forested areas rather than gardens and parks.
Among the comma butterflies, the Gray Comma is distinguished by its particularly prominent white comma mark and overall grayer underside coloration.
